statement: A documented arc of Yolŋu ceremonial/genealogical knowledge functioning as legal-political evidence: the Yirrkala Church Panels (painted collaboratively by Dhuwa and Yirritja clan artists for the Yirrkala Methodist mission church, opened June 1963) asserted ancestral/clan land ownership against unconsulted bauxite mining leases; the Yirrkala Bark Petitions followed, presented to the Australian Parliament August 1963. Milirrpum v Nabalco Pty Ltd (1971) 17 FLR 141 (the "Gove land rights case"), heard before Justice Richard Blackburn, was the first native title litigation in Australian legal history — Yolŋu plaintiffs presented anthropological testimony on clan boundaries and madayin (customary law), and men broke with customary restriction to show sacred rangga emblems to the judge; Blackburn J held the customary system was "subtle and elaborate" but NOT a proprietary interest recognized by Australian common law, upholding terra nullius as then understood — the Yolŋu LOST this case, though it established the practice of admitting Aboriginal oral/genealogical/ceremonial evidence that shaped subsequent land-rights jurisprudence. The 1988 Barunga Statement (presented to PM Bob Hawke, left panel painted by Yolŋu depicting Crocodile Fire and Whale Dreaming narratives) called for land rights, compensation, self-determination, and a treaty; Hawke's 1990 treaty commitment was not fulfilled. Decades later, the Blue Mud Bay determination (2005) and related 2008 High Court decision succeeded where Milirrpum had not: fifty Yolŋu bark paintings (the "Saltwater Collection," led by Djambawa Marawili) were presented as evidence linking clans to coastal/intertidal sea country, with Howard Morphy as anthropological expert and Frances Morphy as expert linguist.

sources.citation: Milirrpum v Nabalco Pty Ltd (1971) 17 FLR 141 (Blackburn J, NT Supreme Court).
Morphy, Frances, et al. "Witness Statements as Cross-Cultural (mis)Communication? Evidence from Blue Mud Bay." Anthropological Forum, 2023.
sources.author: Frances Morphy et al.

does_not_demonstrate: That Milirrpum was a Yolŋu legal victory — it was a loss on the proprietary-interest question, significant instead for establishing the evidentiary practice that later succeeded in Blue Mud Bay decades later
